materials.Guidance: Machinability: good at 28–40 HRC. Traps: small DOC with high feed in hard zones rubs and chips the edge. Chips: trochoidal/dynamic roughing. Burrs: low. Finish: flood gives the best finish; constant engagement and small stepover.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide + TiAlN coating • Coolant: Dry, MQL, or wet (wet = better finish) • Params: Trochoidal roughing, moderate DOC • Traps: Avoid small DOC + high feed in hard zones — rubs, chips edge

materials.Guidance: Machinability: poor. Thermal: low conductivity keeps heat at the edge; a dull edge work-hardens. Chips: 70 bar HPC, never dry (fine swarf is a fire risk). Burrs: moderate; retract before stopping. Finish: low Vc, constant chip load, arc entries.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Uncoated fine-grain carbide or PCD • Coolant: HPC mandatory — NEVER dry cut • Params: Low surface speed, moderate feed per tooth • Traps: Never rub a dull edge — work-hardens surface

materials.Guidance: Machinability: excellent. Thermal: gummy and BUE at low Vc, so run high Vc (300–600). Chips: large polished flutes, flood or air blast, avoid recutting. Burrs: sharp edge, climb mill; thin walls burr on exit. Finish: light 0.1–0.3 mm pass at full Vc.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide or HSS, ZrN optional • Coolant: Flood, MQL, or air • Params: 300–600 m/min, aggressive roughing OK • Traps: Burrs on thin walls and hole edges

materials.Guidance: Machinability: very good, tougher than 6082. Thermal: finishing can drift with heat. Chips: flood or MQL, keep long chips moving. Burrs: fine stubborn burrs, so sharp tools plus a deburr pass. Finish: ZrN or DLC tools, light spring pass.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide, ZrN or DLC coating • Coolant: Flood or MQL • Params: High RPM, moderate feed; conservative vs 6082 • Traps: Thermal drift on finishing; fine stubborn burrs

materials.Guidance: Machinability: good, but high Cu makes forces climb fast. Thermal: keep chips moving. Chips: flood, avoid packing. Burrs: moderate. Finish: conservative feeds vs 6082, sharp tools.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide • Coolant: Flood • Params: Conservative vs 6082; forces climb fast • Traps: High Cu content — keep chips moving

materials.Guidance: Machinability: poor, gummy and stringy. Thermal: strong work hardening, so rubbing or dwell hardens the surface. Chips: flood, peck or chipbreaker. Burrs: heavy; sharp positive tools, climb mill, deburr. Finish: firm feed, skip skimming spring passes.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide, sharp positive rake • Coolant: Flood mandatory • Params: Low speed + high feed — never light feed • Traps: Work-hardens if edge rubs; needs rigid setup + ~50% more power

materials.Guidance: Machinability: fair (~50–70%), wears tools faster than Condition A. Thermal: gummy. Chips: flood, steady feed. Burrs: moderate. Finish: thread mill instead of tap; sharp carbide.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide • Coolant: Flood • Params: Reduce vs Condition A; ~50–70% machinability • Traps: Drilling/tapping hard — use thread mill instead of tap

materials.Guidance: Machinability: best of the 17-4PH states, close to 304. Thermal: gummy, BUE-prone. Chips: flood. Burrs: moderate. Finish: machine before ageing if possible and allow for small dimensional change on ageing.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide • Coolant: Flood • Params: Machines close to 302/304 • Traps: Best machinability of 17-4PH states — machine before aging if possible

materials.Guidance: Machinability: good. Thermal: no major traps. Chips: flood or MQL, easy chips. Burrs: moderate. Finish: good with carbide at steady Vc.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide • Coolant: Flood or MQL • Params: High speed + heavy feed • Traps: None major — straightforward cutting

materials.Guidance: Machinability: fair; wear rises toward 300 HB. Thermal: rigidity matters more than speed. Chips: flood, trochoidal roughing. Burrs: light. Finish: constant engagement, light finish passes.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide or coated • Coolant: Flood • Params: Trochoidal roughing, moderate feed • Traps: Tool wear accelerates near 300 HB; rigidity matters

materials.Guidance: Machinability: poor (363–415 HB). Thermal: a sliding edge work-hardens. Chips: plenty of flood, coated carbide. Burrs: low. Finish: low Vc, moderate feed, no dwell.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide or better (coated) • Coolant: Flood, plenty • Params: Low surface speed, moderate feed • Traps: Never let edge slide — work-hardens

materials.Guidance: Machinability: good. Thermal: heat softens near Tg ~143 °C; moisture causes swelling. Chips: air blast or MQL. Burrs: fuzz and strings, so keep tools sharp. Finish: sharp high-rake carbide.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide, sharp • Coolant: Strong air blast or MQL — avoid flood • Params: 180–230 m/min, moderate feed • Traps: Heat softens/melts (Tg ≈ 143°C); moisture = swelling

materials.Guidance: Machinability: fair, abrasive. Thermal: keep below Tg. Chips: air plus dust extraction (glass dust hazard). Burrs: fibre fuzz. Finish: PCD preferred, climb mill.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide min, PCD preferred • Coolant: Air blast or MQL; suppress dust • Params: Reduce speed (~100–180 m/min), moderate feed • Traps: Highly abrasive; glass dust is a health hazard

materials.Guidance: Machinability: abrasive, PCD required. Thermal: heat builds in the cut. Chips: air plus extraction. Burrs: fibre pull-out and fuzz; climb mill with sharp tools. Finish: lower speed, controlled feed.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: PCD required • Coolant: Air blast or MQL • Params: Lower speed, controlled feed • Traps: Extremely abrasive; avoid fiber pull-out (fuzzy surface)

materials.Guidance: Machinability: good but soft. Thermal: dry before machining; heat swells it. Chips: stringy, so use a chipbreaker and air. Burrs: heavy. Finish: sharp high-rake tools, light cuts.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Sharp carbide, high rake • Coolant: Air blast or minimal fluid — avoid flood • Params: 180–250 m/min • Traps: Dry before machining; chips wrap — use chipbreaker

materials.Guidance: Machinability: difficult at about 45 HRC. Thermal: abrasive, wears tools fast. Chips: flood or HPC. Burrs: moderate. Finish: conservative Vc, rigid setup, thread mill not tap.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide • Coolant: Flood or HPC • Params: Conservative Vc • Traps: Abrasive, thread mill not tap

materials.Guidance: Machinability: fair, gummy. Thermal: work-hardens. Chips: flood, stringy chips. Burrs: heavy. Finish: positive rake and firm feed.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide, sharp positive rake • Coolant: Flood • Params: Low speed + firm feed • Traps: Work-hardens if edge rubs

materials.Guidance: Machinability: better than H1025 (softer, ~33 HRC). Thermal: gummy, BUE-prone. Chips: flood. Burrs: moderate. Finish: sharp carbide, steady feed.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide • Coolant: Flood • Params: Easier than H1025 • Traps: Gummy, BUE

materials.Guidance: Machinability: poor even annealed; carbides are abrasive. Thermal: rapid flank wear. Chips: flood or air. Burrs: low. Finish: coated carbide, moderate Vc; hardened D2 needs hard-milling tooling.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Coated carbide • Coolant: Flood or air • Params: Moderate Vc • Traps: Abrasive carbides, fast flank wear

materials.Guidance: Machinability: good annealed. Thermal: distortion after heat treat, so leave stock. Chips: easy. Burrs: moderate. Finish: good with carbide.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide • Coolant: Flood • Params: Standard steel parameters • Traps: Distorts after heat treat

materials.Guidance: Machinability: very poor. Thermal: severe work hardening and notch wear at the DOC line. Chips: 70 bar HPC, vary DOC between passes. Burrs: heavy. Finish: low Vc, rigid setup, fresh edge for finishing.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Carbide or ceramic • Coolant: HPC mandatory • Params: Very low Vc, constant chip load • Traps: Work hardening, notch wear

materials.Guidance: Machinability: excellent. Thermal: low heat tolerance, little coolant needed. Chips: clean, air blast. Burrs: low. Finish: sharp tools give a very good finish.
materials.Notes: • Tooling: Sharp carbide, high rake • Coolant: Air blast • Params: High Vc, moderate feed • Traps: Low heat tolerance

cycles.Best For: Every drilled hole above 3mm where position accuracy matters
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: No peck or deep-hole logic
cycles.Gotchas: A worn spot drill causes drill wander — replace early
cycles.Key Capabilities: Simple spot drill; quick positioning
cycles.Tips: Spot only as deep as the drill's point — going deeper wastes time and dulls the spot drill

cycles.Best For: Shallow holes in aluminum, plastics, mild steel
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: No chip breaking; poor in deep holes; chips can pack in flutes
cycles.Gotchas: Chips wrapping on the drill cause hole oversize and drill breakage
cycles.Key Capabilities: Direct drill cycle; efficient for L/D < 3; fast cycle time
cycles.Tips: For L/D > 3, use chip break instead

cycles.Best For: Holes with L/D between 3 and 5, gummy materials (SS, aluminum)
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Slower cycle time; multiple retracts add up
cycles.Gotchas: Too small a peck depth wastes cycle time — too large packs chips
cycles.Key Capabilities: G83-style peck; full retract between pecks; clear chip evacuation
cycles.Tips: Reduce peck depth as you go deeper (2×D shallow, 1×D mid, 0.5×D deep)

cycles.Best For: Deep bores, coolant channels, oil passages
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Significant cycle time; risk of drill wander at depth
cycles.Gotchas: Without high pressure coolant, chips don't evacuate and the drill breaks
cycles.Key Capabilities: Optimized peck schedule; full retract option; chip evacuation priority
cycles.Tips: Start with a spot drill and pilot drill; step up to full size

cycles.Best For: Bearing bores, dowel pin holes, precision fits
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Must pre-drill; cannot plunge into solid; max 0.1×D radial
cycles.Gotchas: Never reverse a reamer while still in the hole — it dulls instantly
cycles.Key Capabilities: Tight tolerance finishing (H7 typically); good surface finish
cycles.Tips: Pre-drill with 0.2–0.3 mm stock for the reamer; run low RPM

cycles.Best For: Threads in aluminum, mild steel, plastics, soft stainless
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Not for >35 HRC; tap breakage risk in difficult materials
cycles.Gotchas: Broken taps are the #1 nightmare — use thread milling in hard materials
cycles.Key Capabilities: Rigid tapping; floating tap support; fast cycle
cycles.Tips: Use form taps in aluminum and mild steel — stronger and chip-free

cycles.Best For: Large precision bores, bearing seats, cylinder bores
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Single pass per tool; slow; requires rigid setup
cycles.Gotchas: Chatter is common — reduce overhang, increase rigidity
cycles.Key Capabilities: Single-point boring; adjustable diameter; tight tolerance
cycles.Tips: Leave 0.3–0.5 mm stock after drilling for the boring pass

cycles.Best For: Through-holes needing counterbore on the back side
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Limited tool access; fragile tooling; low speed required
cycles.Gotchas: Tool entry through the pilot hole can crash — verify clearance in simulation
cycles.Key Capabilities: Undercut access from below; reached through a smaller pilot hole
cycles.Tips: Run very conservative RPM — back boring bars are the most fragile of all

cycles.Best For: Holes larger than your largest drill, deep pockets, ramping into pockets
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Requires helical-capable tool; slower than a full-size drill
cycles.Gotchas: Non-center-cutting end mills will rub — verify before running
cycles.Key Capabilities: Helical interpolation; reduced tool load; uses smaller tool for larger hole
cycles.Tips: Helix angle should be <5° for shallow ramps, 2–3° for deep

cycles.Best For: Hardened steel, stainless, titanium, large threads, threads near shoulders
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Multiple passes; slower than tapping; requires full profile tool
cycles.Gotchas: Feed must be adjusted for the cutter's circular path — AFR formula
cycles.Key Capabilities: Best for >35 HRC; any thread size; no broken taps
cycles.Purpose: Threads in hard materials where tapping fails
cycles.Tips: Always take 2–3 spring passes at final depth for thread quality

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Only round geometry; not for irregular shapes
cycles.Gotchas: Small end mills deflect in a circular path — use the largest tool that fits
cycles.Key Capabilities: Efficient circular path; good for bores and round pockets
cycles.Tips: Use helical entry, not straight plunge

cycles.Best For: Oil passages, hydraulic manifolds, deep cooling channels
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Requires specialized gun drill tooling; very high coolant pressure
cycles.Gotchas: Without proper pressure and flow, the drill seizes
cycles.Key Capabilities: Straightest holes possible; excellent surface finish; deep reach
cycles.Tips: Pilot hole must be precise — gun drills follow the pilot

cycles.Best For: Angled holes on aerospace parts, complex fixtures
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Complex programming; collision risk; slower than 3-axis
cycles.Gotchas: Tool-axis misalignment causes severe rub and tool breakage
cycles.Key Capabilities: Simultaneous 5-axis interpolation; angled holes; compound angles
cycles.Purpose: Helical drilling on angled or complex geometry
cycles.Tips: Verify tool axis vectors in simulation before cutting

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Does not follow sloped walls; stepped sides on non-vertical walls
cycles.Gotchas: Sloped walls need 3D strategies — Pocket Milling leaves steps
cycles.Key Capabilities: Standard stepover; efficient roughing for 2D pockets
cycles.Tips: Use trochoidal entry to avoid full-width cuts

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Does not account for surface slope; constant Z depth only
cycles.Gotchas: For sloped profiles, switch to 3D ISO Machining
cycles.Key Capabilities: Lead-in/out with arcs; clean profile
cycles.Tips: Use ramp or helical entry, not plunge

cycles.Best For: Chamfering or profiling edges of 3D parts
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Limited to contour; no surface finish control
cycles.Gotchas: Path follows the model's edge — pencil mill cleanup may be needed
cycles.Key Capabilities: Profile follows 3D edge; auto-detects edges
cycles.Tips: Use for edge breaks on complex 3D parts

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Fragile tool; limited depth; requires pre-machined slot
cycles.Gotchas: T-slot cutters break easily — never plunge, always ramp in
cycles.Key Capabilities: Dedicated T-slot geometry; undercut access
cycles.Tips: Rough the neck with a smaller end mill first

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Only for chamfer geometry; not for surfacing
cycles.Gotchas: Sharp corners cause tool spikes — enter with arcs
cycles.Key Capabilities: Follows 3D edges; automatic chamfer; consistent width
cycles.Tips: Use 45° chamfer mill for standard edges

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Path overlap can cause marks on walls
cycles.Gotchas: Visible marks at direction changes — overlap carefully
cycles.Key Capabilities: Multiple angle passes; follows inclined geometry
cycles.Tips: Reduce stepover at final pass for finish

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Does not smooth transitions; visible steps
cycles.Gotchas: For a smooth blend, chain rough with inclined pocket, finish with Z-Level
cycles.Key Capabilities: Steps down along slope; follows inclination
cycles.Tips: Use 3D Z-Level Shape Finishing to finish inclined walls

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Only rectangular geometry
cycles.Gotchas: Sharp internal corners require smaller tool or corner rest
cycles.Key Capabilities: Optimized rectangular path; efficient stepover
cycles.Tips: Use trochoidal entry from the middle

cycles.Best For: Cleaning up after large tools, corner access
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Slower calculation; needs a reference operation; can miss corners
cycles.Gotchas: No reference = no rest. Verify stock model is up to date
cycles.Key Capabilities: Detects previous tool's remaining stock; auto-limits to rest areas
cycles.Purpose: Remove material left by previous operations
cycles.Tips: Always reference the previous roughing operation

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Does not follow curved surfaces; flat only
cycles.Gotchas: Chatter on large face mills — reduce RPM or use positive rake inserts
cycles.Key Capabilities: Face mill or end mill; efficient coverage; single-plane
cycles.Tips: 70–80% stepover of cutter diameter for best finish

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: No intelligent adaptation; only re-runs
cycles.Gotchas: If stock or part changes, playback doesn't adapt
cycles.Key Capabilities: Repeat known-good paths exactly; no re-calculation
cycles.Tips: Use for high-mix, low-volume jobs where the path is proven

cycles.Best For: Hardened steel, tool steel, deep cavities with limited access
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Slow MRR; requires specialized plunge mill
cycles.Gotchas: Slowest roughing method — only use when nothing else works
cycles.Key Capabilities: Very rigid (only Z-force); no side deflection
cycles.Purpose: Roughing difficult materials with Z-axis-only motion
cycles.Tips: Use a plunge mill with a chip-splitting tip

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Not for finishing; leaves stock; requires CAM experience
cycles.Gotchas: Chip thinning is critical — at 5–10% WOC, feed must be raised significantly
cycles.Key Capabilities: Trochoidal-capable; HSC/HPC optimized; high MRR; dynamic feed
cycles.Tips: Use bull nose (corner radius) tools — stronger edge, better chip thinning

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Does NOT account for sloped surfaces — constant stepover on steep areas creates cusps
cycles.Gotchas: Steep areas will need 3D ISO Machining or Z-Level to fix cusps
cycles.Key Capabilities: Precise finishing of individual surfaces; ISO-curve alignment
cycles.Purpose: Follow a contour profile along a surface
cycles.Tips: Only for gently sloped surfaces — switch to ISO Machining for steep walls

cycles.Best For: Vertical walls, deep ribs, steep features
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Stepped appearance on slopes; many Z levels needed for smooth finish
cycles.Gotchas: On slopes, this creates visible steps — combine with ISO Machining
cycles.Key Capabilities: References curved bottom surfaces; paths nestle optimally along wall/bottom edge
cycles.Tips: Use small Z stepdown on curved bottoms — smaller step, smoother finish

cycles.Best For: Complex 3D surfaces, molds, curved organic shapes
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Requires clean surface topology; can be slower than Z-level
cycles.Gotchas: Slower than Z-level — only use where stepover smoothness matters
cycles.Key Capabilities: Follows U/V ISO curves; calculates smaller stepdowns on slopes automatically
cycles.Tips: Clean up your surface model — messy topology confuses ISO curves

cycles.Best For: Special finishing paths on unique features
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Manual path creation; less automation; error-prone
cycles.Gotchas: Path errors cause crashes — verify in simulation
cycles.Key Capabilities: User-defined path geometry; arbitrary tool motions
cycles.Tips: Only use when no standard cycle fits

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Does NOT follow slopes; flat only
cycles.Gotchas: Does not clean up corner fillets — follow with pencil mill if needed
cycles.Key Capabilities: Auto-detects planar surfaces; efficient pocket strategy
cycles.Tips: Combine with 3D Z-Level Shape Finishing for wall + floor

cycles.Best For: Castings, forgings, weldments with irregular stock
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Complex setup; slower calculation; no trochoidal
cycles.Gotchas: Slower than 3D Optimized Roughing — only for irregular stock
cycles.Key Capabilities: Any stock shape; multi-directional passes
cycles.Tips: Verify stock model is accurate to avoid air cutting

cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Does not follow curved bottom; requires rework on curved surfaces
cycles.Gotchas: On curved surfaces, this leaves visible steps — use 3D Z-Level Shape Finishing
cycles.Key Capabilities: Standard Z-level stepping; predictable; straightforward
cycles.Tips: Small stepdown on slopes for smoother finish

cycles.Best For: Cleaning up after roughing, reaching deep corners
cycles.Drawbacks / Limits: Needs reference tool; can miss corners
cycles.Gotchas: Always verify stock model is current
cycles.Key Capabilities: Auto-detects rest material; limits path to leftover areas
cycles.Purpose: Remove remaining stock after previous operations
cycles.Tips: Use progressively smaller tools (12mm > 6mm > 3mm)

cycles.Best For: Cleaning corners after larger tools, fillet cleanup

cycles.Gotchas: Small tools break easily — reduce feed
cycles.Key Capabilities: Targets corners left by larger tools; precise corner removal
cycles.Tips: Use the largest tool that fits the corner radius

cycles.Gotchas: Fragile tooling — reduce feed
cycles.Key Capabilities: Cleans internal corners; follows tight radii
cycles.Tips: Use after larger tool finishes — pencil cleans the corners

cycles.Key Capabilities: Combines strategies; covers entire part

formulas.doc: RPM = Vc×1000 ÷ (π×D) · Feed = RPM × Fz × Z · MRR = Feed × DOC × WOC ÷ 1000
formulas.name: Milling: RPM, feed, MRR

inputs.label: Programmed feed at tool centre mm/min

formulas.doc: Internal: F = Fedge·(Dh−Dc)/Dh · External: F = Fedge·(Dh+Dc)/Dh · θ = atan(p ÷ (π·(Dh−Dc))). Path-diameter is the tool-centre circle.

inputs.label: Helical pitch / ramp drop mm per rev

formulas.name: Helical interpolation: edge feed (internal and external)

formulas.doc: φ = acos(1 − 2ae/D) · Fz = hm ÷ sin φ for ae < 50% D (no correction above)
formulas.name: True radial chip thinning / trochoidal

out.else: Reduce ap, use variable-helix / short tooling
out.label: Advice

formulas.doc: Pc = MRR·kc ÷ (60 000·0.8) · T = 9549·P ÷ RPM. Compare with your machine spindle rating.

inputs.label: Specific cutting force kc N/mm² (typical, verify)

formulas.name: Spindle power and torque

formulas.doc: Deff = 2·√(ap·(D − ap)). At shallow ap the cutting edge is on a smaller diameter, so use Deff for RPM.
formulas.name: Ballnose effective diameter (Deff)

formulas.doc: Cut tap drill ≈ d − P · form tap ≈ d − 0.5P · pitch Ø = d − 0.6495P
formulas.name: Tap drill and pitch diameter

formulas.doc: Reamer stock 0.2–0.3 mm, ~½ drill Vc, ~2× drill feed/rev, flood. Boring stock 0.3–0.5 mm, L/D ≤ 4, single-point feed 0.05–0.15 mm/rev.
formulas.name: Reaming and boring set-up

formulas.doc: Cusp height h = Ra × k ÷ 1000 (mm). Stepover s = 2√(h·(D − h)). k = 1 means cusp height equals the Ra target (conservative); k = 4 means the scallop Ra is cusp ÷ 4 (Ra ≈ h/4 handbook convention). The default k is set in Library → Setup.

inputs.hint: 1 = cusp height equals Ra target (conservative). 4 = classic Ra ≈ cusp/4.
inputs.label: Cusp / Ra multiplier

formulas.name: Ball nose: stepover for target Ra

cycle_reference.best_for: Every drilled hole above 3mm where position accuracy matters
cycle_reference.capabilities: Simple spot drill; quick positioning
cycle_reference.gotchas: A worn spot drill causes drill wander — replace early
cycle_reference.tips: Spot only as deep as the drill's point — going deeper wastes time and dulls the spot drill

cycle_reference.best_for: Shallow holes in aluminum, plastics, mild steel
cycle_reference.capabilities: Direct drill cycle; efficient for L/D < 3; fast cycle time
cycle_reference.drawbacks: No chip breaking; poor in deep holes; chips can pack in flutes
cycle_reference.gotchas: Chips wrapping on the drill cause hole oversize and drill breakage
cycle_reference.tips: For L/D > 3, use chip break instead

cycle_reference.best_for: Holes with L/D between 3 and 5, gummy materials (SS, aluminum)
cycle_reference.capabilities: G83-style peck; full retract between pecks; clear chip evacuation
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Slower cycle time; multiple retracts add up
cycle_reference.gotchas: Too small a peck depth wastes cycle time — too large packs chips
cycle_reference.tips: Reduce peck depth as you go deeper (2×D shallow, 1×D mid, 0.5×D deep)

cycle_reference.best_for: Deep bores, coolant channels, oil passages
cycle_reference.capabilities: Optimized peck schedule; full retract option; chip evacuation priority
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Significant cycle time; risk of drill wander at depth
cycle_reference.gotchas: Without high pressure coolant, chips don't evacuate and the drill breaks
cycle_reference.tips: Start with a spot drill and pilot drill; step up to full size

cycle_reference.best_for: Bearing bores, dowel pin holes, precision fits
cycle_reference.capabilities: Tight tolerance finishing (H7 typically); good surface finish
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Must pre-drill; cannot plunge into solid; max 0.1×D radial
cycle_reference.gotchas: Never reverse a reamer while still in the hole — it dulls instantly
cycle_reference.tips: Pre-drill with 0.2–0.3 mm stock for the reamer; run low RPM

cycle_reference.best_for: Threads in aluminum, mild steel, plastics, soft stainless
cycle_reference.capabilities: Rigid tapping; floating tap support; fast cycle
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Not for >35 HRC; tap breakage risk in difficult materials
cycle_reference.gotchas: Broken taps are the #1 nightmare — use thread milling in hard materials
cycle_reference.tips: Use form taps in aluminum and mild steel — stronger and chip-free

cycle_reference.best_for: Large precision bores, bearing seats, cylinder bores
cycle_reference.capabilities: Single-point boring; adjustable diameter; tight tolerance
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Single pass per tool; slow; requires rigid setup
cycle_reference.gotchas: Chatter is common — reduce overhang, increase rigidity
cycle_reference.tips: Leave 0.3–0.5 mm stock after drilling for the boring pass

cycle_reference.best_for: Through-holes needing counterbore on the back side
cycle_reference.capabilities: Undercut access from below; reached through a smaller pilot hole
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Limited tool access; fragile tooling; low speed required
cycle_reference.gotchas: Tool entry through the pilot hole can crash — verify clearance in simulation
cycle_reference.tips: Run very conservative RPM — back boring bars are the most fragile of all

cycle_reference.best_for: Holes larger than your largest drill, deep pockets, ramping into pockets
cycle_reference.capabilities: Helical interpolation; reduced tool load; uses smaller tool for larger hole
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Requires helical-capable tool; slower than a full-size drill
cycle_reference.gotchas: Non-center-cutting end mills will rub — verify before running
cycle_reference.tips: Helix angle should be <5° for shallow ramps, 2–3° for deep

cycle_reference.purpose: Threads in hard materials where tapping fails
cycle_reference.best_for: Hardened steel, stainless, titanium, large threads, threads near shoulders
cycle_reference.capabilities: Best for >35 HRC; any thread size; no broken taps
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Multiple passes; slower than tapping; requires full profile tool
cycle_reference.gotchas: Feed must be adjusted for the cutter's circular path — AFR formula
cycle_reference.tips: Always take 2–3 spring passes at final depth for thread quality

cycle_reference.capabilities: Efficient circular path; good for bores and round pockets
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Only round geometry; not for irregular shapes
cycle_reference.gotchas: Small end mills deflect in a circular path — use the largest tool that fits
cycle_reference.tips: Use helical entry, not straight plunge

cycle_reference.best_for: Oil passages, hydraulic manifolds, deep cooling channels
cycle_reference.capabilities: Straightest holes possible; excellent surface finish; deep reach
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Requires specialized gun drill tooling; very high coolant pressure
cycle_reference.gotchas: Without proper pressure and flow, the drill seizes
cycle_reference.tips: Pilot hole must be precise — gun drills follow the pilot

cycle_reference.purpose: Helical drilling on angled or complex geometry
cycle_reference.best_for: Angled holes on aerospace parts, complex fixtures
cycle_reference.capabilities: Simultaneous 5-axis interpolation; angled holes; compound angles
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Complex programming; collision risk; slower than 3-axis
cycle_reference.gotchas: Tool-axis misalignment causes severe rub and tool breakage
cycle_reference.tips: Verify tool axis vectors in simulation before cutting

cycle_reference.capabilities: Standard stepover; efficient roughing for 2D pockets
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Does not follow sloped walls; stepped sides on non-vertical walls
cycle_reference.gotchas: Sloped walls need 3D strategies — Pocket Milling leaves steps
cycle_reference.tips: Use trochoidal entry to avoid full-width cuts

cycle_reference.capabilities: Lead-in/out with arcs; clean profile
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Does not account for surface slope; constant Z depth only
cycle_reference.gotchas: For sloped profiles, switch to 3D ISO Machining
cycle_reference.tips: Use ramp or helical entry, not plunge

cycle_reference.best_for: Chamfering or profiling edges of 3D parts
cycle_reference.capabilities: Profile follows 3D edge; auto-detects edges
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Limited to contour; no surface finish control
cycle_reference.gotchas: Path follows the model's edge — pencil mill cleanup may be needed
cycle_reference.tips: Use for edge breaks on complex 3D parts

cycle_reference.capabilities: Dedicated T-slot geometry; undercut access
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Fragile tool; limited depth; requires pre-machined slot
cycle_reference.gotchas: T-slot cutters break easily — never plunge, always ramp in
cycle_reference.tips: Rough the neck with a smaller end mill first

cycle_reference.capabilities: Follows 3D edges; automatic chamfer; consistent width
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Only for chamfer geometry; not for surfacing
cycle_reference.gotchas: Sharp corners cause tool spikes — enter with arcs
cycle_reference.tips: Use 45° chamfer mill for standard edges

cycle_reference.capabilities: Multiple angle passes; follows inclined geometry
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Path overlap can cause marks on walls
cycle_reference.gotchas: Visible marks at direction changes — overlap carefully
cycle_reference.tips: Reduce stepover at final pass for finish

cycle_reference.capabilities: Steps down along slope; follows inclination
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Does not smooth transitions; visible steps
cycle_reference.gotchas: For a smooth blend, chain rough with inclined pocket, finish with Z-Level
cycle_reference.tips: Use 3D Z-Level Shape Finishing to finish inclined walls

cycle_reference.capabilities: Optimized rectangular path; efficient stepover
cycle_reference.gotchas: Sharp internal corners require smaller tool or corner rest
cycle_reference.tips: Use trochoidal entry from the middle

cycle_reference.purpose: Remove material left by previous operations
cycle_reference.best_for: Cleaning up after large tools, corner access
cycle_reference.capabilities: Detects previous tool's remaining stock; auto-limits to rest areas
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Slower calculation; needs a reference operation; can miss corners
cycle_reference.gotchas: No reference = no rest. Verify stock model is up to date
cycle_reference.tips: Always reference the previous roughing operation

cycle_reference.capabilities: Face mill or end mill; efficient coverage; single-plane
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Does not follow curved surfaces; flat only
cycle_reference.gotchas: Chatter on large face mills — reduce RPM or use positive rake inserts
cycle_reference.tips: 70–80% stepover of cutter diameter for best finish

cycle_reference.capabilities: Repeat known-good paths exactly; no re-calculation
cycle_reference.gotchas: If stock or part changes, playback doesn't adapt
cycle_reference.tips: Use for high-mix, low-volume jobs where the path is proven

cycle_reference.purpose: Roughing difficult materials with Z-axis-only motion
cycle_reference.best_for: Hardened steel, tool steel, deep cavities with limited access
cycle_reference.capabilities: Very rigid (only Z-force); no side deflection
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Slow MRR; requires specialized plunge mill
cycle_reference.gotchas: Slowest roughing method — only use when nothing else works
cycle_reference.tips: Use a plunge mill with a chip-splitting tip

cycle_reference.capabilities: Trochoidal-capable; HSC/HPC optimized; high MRR; dynamic feed
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Not for finishing; leaves stock; requires CAM experience
cycle_reference.gotchas: Chip thinning is critical — at 5–10% WOC, feed must be raised significantly
cycle_reference.tips: Use bull nose (corner radius) tools — stronger edge, better chip thinning

cycle_reference.purpose: Follow a contour profile along a surface
cycle_reference.capabilities: Precise finishing of individual surfaces; ISO-curve alignment
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Does NOT account for sloped surfaces — constant stepover on steep areas creates cusps
cycle_reference.gotchas: Steep areas will need 3D ISO Machining or Z-Level to fix cusps
cycle_reference.tips: Only for gently sloped surfaces — switch to ISO Machining for steep walls

cycle_reference.best_for: Vertical walls, deep ribs, steep features
cycle_reference.capabilities: References curved bottom surfaces; paths nestle optimally along wall/bottom edge
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Stepped appearance on slopes; many Z levels needed for smooth finish
cycle_reference.gotchas: On slopes, this creates visible steps — combine with ISO Machining
cycle_reference.tips: Use small Z stepdown on curved bottoms — smaller step, smoother finish

cycle_reference.best_for: Complex 3D surfaces, molds, curved organic shapes
cycle_reference.capabilities: Follows U/V ISO curves; calculates smaller stepdowns on slopes automatically
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Requires clean surface topology; can be slower than Z-level
cycle_reference.gotchas: Slower than Z-level — only use where stepover smoothness matters
cycle_reference.tips: Clean up your surface model — messy topology confuses ISO curves

cycle_reference.best_for: Special finishing paths on unique features
cycle_reference.capabilities: User-defined path geometry; arbitrary tool motions
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Manual path creation; less automation; error-prone
cycle_reference.gotchas: Path errors cause crashes — verify in simulation
cycle_reference.tips: Only use when no standard cycle fits

cycle_reference.capabilities: Auto-detects planar surfaces; efficient pocket strategy
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Does NOT follow slopes; flat only
cycle_reference.gotchas: Does not clean up corner fillets — follow with pencil mill if needed
cycle_reference.tips: Combine with 3D Z-Level Shape Finishing for wall + floor

cycle_reference.best_for: Castings, forgings, weldments with irregular stock
cycle_reference.capabilities: Any stock shape; multi-directional passes
cycle_reference.drawbacks: Complex setup; slower calculation; no trochoidal
cycle_reference.gotchas: Slower than 3D Optimized Roughing — only for irregular stock
cycle_reference.tips: Verify stock model is accurate to avoid air cutting

cycle_reference.capabilities: Standard Z-level stepping; predictable; straightforward

show 'Arc in and arc out; no dwell at contact'
show 'Feed −30 % for the last 1×Ø before breakthrough'
set toolpath = 'dynamic'
clamp ap <= max_ap_mm
show 'Reduce ap or ae' with Pc and T
show 'Vary ap between passes (notch line)'
block 'Diamond/DLC tool in ferrous or Ti/Ni alloy'
show 'Corner feed −30 % or use a smaller rest tool'
show 'Reference tool Ø ≥ 1.5 × current Ø'
show 'Leave 0.2–0.5 mm stock by Ø band'
show 'Floor finish with corner-radius tool, ae ≤ 0.5·Ø'
clamp ap <= flute_length
show 'Step down alternately both sides; light ae; climb'
show 'Expect exit burrs; plan a deburr pass'
clamp rpm <= rpm_max; keep fz; show real Vc
show 'Constant engagement; no full-width moves'
set fz = fz * h_min / hex
block 'Use coated carbide'
block 'Thread mill instead of tap'
clamp ae <= 0.05 * D; show 'Air or dry with coated tool'
show 'Semi-finish to equal stock first'
show 'Tilt 5–15° off ball centre; rpm on Deff'
show '0.1–0.3 mm pass at full Vc'

rules_engine.trigger_expression: op == 'finish' and tolerance_tight and not work_hardening

block spring pass; show 'Firm feed instead of a skim'
set coolant = 'HPC'; block dry
set coolant = 'flood' (minimum)
show 'Air blast or MQL; avoid flood (swelling)'
show 'Dust extraction: glass/carbon dust hazard'
scale Vc * 0.75
set coolant = 'through-spindle'
show 'MQL or air for finishing'
clamp Vc <= 2 * typical_Vc; clamp fz <= 2 * typical_fz; show 'Catalogue value capped at 2× typical'

items.text: Upload the catalogue list (see the Catalogues item notes) — DC Swiss, Horn, ITC, drill maker(s), reamer, thread-mill and face-mill makers, plus any others
After upload: audit every tool against its catalogue row (Ø, flutes, flute/cutting length, corner radius, coating) and report differences without changing anything
Add manufacturer Vc / Fz rows (tag MFR) to the cheat sheet beside Ref and Your values
Decide the 4 end mills with conflicting lengths: 2 AL (12 vs 8), 60 AL (25 vs 22.5), 11 DM (9 vs 20), 21 DM (18 vs 32)
Check long-reach HRBG ball-nose tools ("× 14 BALLNOSE" etc.): length may be reach/neck, not flute length
Give thread length for each thread mill (Max DOC currently equals cutter Ø) so Cutting Length can be filled
Fix odd Max DOC values: reamers (e.g. 1 RM = 0.1), 14 HSS (108), 36 CD (62, no length in description)
Review Library → Tooling audit; decide which flagged values to change (DC Swiss diameters unverified)
Keep logging cuts (especially Good/Stable) so Your columns and Δ feed fill in
Compare Ref vs Your; mark rows where your values should become the baseline
Send screenshots of hyperMILL cycle settings pages so the per-cycle parameter list can be replaced with yours
After catalogues: re-run audit and update the Library; refresh the "What changed" and User Guide text
Live database: in the Google Sheet use CNC Shop → Set write key; then on the PC with the latest data Settings → Live database → enter the key → Save & test → reload → Upload this PC’s data
Once the live database holds your data, delete cnc-library-2026-10-12.json from the GitHub repo (it is public and holds every cut)
Check the new ISO standard band tables (median of each group’s materials) and add a material override only where a material needs different numbers
Add “Show only when” rules to the other cycle pages (Cycles → Cycle pages → field → more); Z-level vertical infeed is done
Confirm the cycle tree: 3D Arbitrary Roughing has the same Trochoidal / Traditional / High feed sub-cycles as 3D Optimised Roughing; Pocket, 3D Plunge Roughing and the “Standard” 3D contour were kept
Profiles: decide who gets admin / editor, then create accounts (2-digit account, 3-digit PIN) — framework is in place
Done: bands per ISO standard with material overrides; square + corner-radius end mills merged; Ø10–15.99 split; RPM / feed shown per Ø
Done: Family › hyperMILL cycle › Operation › Sub-cycle — Log cut only offers valid paths
Done: cycle page fields can depend on an earlier choice, on any tab (picked in the page editor)
Done: factors switchable (Settings → Factors); stale ae / ap note fixed; calculator shows the cutter type; “How to read the tables” rewritten
Done: every result can be typed to work backwards; calculator formulas editable on the Formulas page; engine formulas listed
Done: one live database for every PC (Google Sheet + Apps Script); Setup sheet page removed

entries.to:
TEST PROMPT EDIT>
You are a CNC machining assistant for one machinist (metric, hyperMILL CAM, Mazak Variaxis i-500 / Hurco VMX42UDi / Quaser machines). Each question arrives with an APP CONTEXT block the app has already resolved: the tools matched (e.g. "10mm BX" = every BX tool of Ø10 — treat them as one choice and name the codes), the material record, any setup facts, the CHEAT SHEET rows (manufacturer / your_logs / calibrated / typical) and the LOGGED CUTS for those tools. Use it first; call tools only for anything missing.
Sub-cycles: hyperMILL cycles are a tree — family › operation › sub-cycle (e.g. Roughing (3D) › Rough › Trochoidal). If the user's question names a sub-cycle, prefer tagged cuts over baseline. If it names a family only, present the sub-cycles and say which one your number comes from. Never use a cut tagged with one sub-cycle as evidence for a sibling sub-cycle. Source tiers in the context: DB-SUB (verified tagged cuts, this exact tool + sub-cycle) › DB-SUB-FAM (same tool suffix) › DB › MFR › MFR≈ › CAL › BASE.
Source order — always say which one each number comes from:
 1. YOUR VERIFIED LOGS — cuts with verified:true and result Good/Stable/Quick/Good Finish. Logged cuts WITHOUT verified:true are reference only: you may show them for comparison, but never recommend their numbers as the value, and say they are unverified. Bad/Heavy are warnings.
 2. MANUFACTURER catalogue data (cheat sheet "manufacturer"; "estimated": true means scaled from another material or a similar tool — say "manufacturer-based estimate").
 3. CALIBRATED (model fitted to the user's logs) and TYPICAL (published/typical starting values).
 4. Your own general machining knowledge — allowed when 1–3 are missing or to sanity-check, but label it "general knowledge, not from a catalogue". You cannot browse the web; never claim you looked something up online.
When there are no logged cuts for the case, still give a concrete recommendation: pick the most trustworthy available source, then adjust for the setup.
SETUP ADJUSTMENTS: a workpiece projecting far from the vice (e.g. 200 mm) is the weakest link — it chatters before the tool does. Then: prefer dynamic/trochoidal roughing (hyperMILL MAXX/optimised) with low radial engagement (ae ≈ 5–8 % of Ø), keep ap moderate and step down in levels starting at the top, climb mill, reduce feed per tooth ~20–30 % from the clamped-solid value, keep RPM so Vc sits at the low end of the range, avoid full-width slotting, rough the top of the part first while it is stiffest, and suggest supporting it (jack/support, tailstock, deeper clamping, stub fixture, or machining in two setups). Long TOOL stick-out (L/D > 4) likewise: reduce ae and fz, or use a necked tool. Never exceed the machine spindle limit (cheat-sheet RPM already respects it). Feed = RPM × Fz × flutes; RPM = Vc × 1000 / (π × D).
ANSWER FORMAT (markdown): start with a one-line verdict. Then "### Start here" as a table: Parameter | Value | Source (Vc, RPM, Fz, Feed, ap, ae, strategy/cycle, coolant). Then "### Compared" — a short table of the sources available (manufacturer / your logs / calibrated / typical) with RPM, Fz and feed. Then "### Because of your setup" with 2–5 bullets. Add "### Check" with the calc results (MRR, chip thickness, power vs spindle) when you computed them. Finish with what to log after the cut. Keep it tight.

Then "### Compared" — a short table of the sources available (manufacturer / your logs / calibrated / typical) with RPM, Fz and feed. Then "### Because of your setup" with 2–5 bullets. Add "### Check" with the calc results (MRR, chip thickness, power vs spindle) when you computed them. Finish with what to log after the cut. Keep it tight.
